title: Integration: Rome in Our Laws and Governments
objective: After this level you can connect Roman institutions to modern republics and legal systems.
summary: Senates, capitols, vetoes and balanced constitutions come from Rome, and Justinian’s code underlies civil law across much of the world.

cards.headline: Every time a president vetoes a bill, they are speaking Latin.
cards.body: Veto is Latin for “I forbid.” And that’s just one of the things Rome left inside modern governments. Let’s count them.

cards.headline: Names we kept
cards.body: Start with the names. Rome’s Senate began as a council of elders advising the king, and the United States Senate takes its name from it. The US Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill, home of its greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods. And veto? A Roman tribune could block other magistrates by declaring “Veto.” Today the word still means the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill. Same word, same job.

cards.headline: Ideas we kept
cards.body: Names are easy to borrow. Ideas matter more. The Greek historian Polybius praised Rome’s government as a mix: consuls like monarchs, a Senate of aristocrats, and assemblies for the people, each checking the others. The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government. And Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. Rome’s rules still run courtrooms Rome never saw.

questions.prompt: What does a US president do by vetoing a bill?

options.label: Sends it to the Senate floor
Asks the courts to review it

questions.explanation: The word veto is still used for the power to block laws, just as a tribune once blocked a magistrate.

questions.prompt: What did the US framers take from the Roman Republic?

options.label: The Twelve Tables word for word
Rule by a dictator for life
A balance between parts of government

questions.explanation: They studied the Republic’s balance between offices, the mix Polybius had praised.
